prompt: The filtered scan for 1 October returned 738 items out of 34,100. What does AWS charge it for?

choices.text: The 738 items it returned
choices.why: That would be true if the filter ran before the read. It runs after.

choices.text: Every item it read, the whole table, as the unfiltered scan
choices.why: Right: 364.5 read units either way.

choices.text: Nothing, because a filtered scan is free when it uses `--select COUNT`
choices.why: `COUNT` leaves the items out of the answer; DynamoDB still reads and charges every one.

choices.text: One page, since the answer is under 1 MB
choices.why: Pages are measured on what is read, not on what comes back; there were three.

prompt: `describe-table` answered `TableSizeBytes` 0 for a table of 34,100 items. What is the right conclusion?

choices.text: The items are empty apart from their keys, which `TableSizeBytes` does not count
choices.why: The program measured almost 3 MB of them. An empty item still has its key bytes.

choices.text: moto measures nothing; AWS refreshes it every few hours
choices.why: Right. On either side it is not a way to watch a table grow.

choices.text: The table is in on-demand mode, which reports a size only when provisioned
choices.why: The billing mode does not change what `describe-table` reports.

prompt: An eventually consistent scan page read 12,288 bytes of items. How many read units does it cost?
hint: Blocks of 4 KB, rounded up, and half a unit per block for an eventually consistent read.

prompt: The 364.5-unit scan runs every five minutes for a 30-day month, at 0.1875 dollars per million read units. How many dollars is that, to the cent?
hint: Count the scans first: 12 an hour.

prompt: A query on the table `quitanda` filters on `order_day`, and an index `by-day` exists. Does DynamoDB use the index?

choices.text: Yes, when the index would read fewer items
choices.why: That is a planner's judgement, and DynamoDB makes none.

choices.text: Only for an eventually consistent read, since the index is one
choices.why: Consistency has nothing to do with it; the request decides.

choices.text: No: a read uses an index only when the request names it
choices.why: Right. `--index-name by-day` is what makes it a read of the index.

choices.text: Yes, after the backfill has finished copying the table
choices.why: The backfill makes the index usable, not automatic.

prompt: Match each projection to what an item of the index carries.

pairs.right: The index's keys and the table's

right_distractors: Only the index's keys, without the table's

prompt: An app writes an order and immediately queries `by-day` with `--consistent-read` to show it. What happens?
hint: How does a write reach a global index?

choices.text: The query waits until the index has the order, and then answers
choices.why: There is no waiting mode; the request is refused.

choices.text: It is refused: a global index is only eventually consistent
choices.why: Right. moto refused it with the same message AWS uses.

choices.text: It answers, at twice the read units
choices.why: Double units buy strong consistency on a table, never on a global index.

prompt: Which of these does a global secondary index add to Quitanda's bill? Choose every one.
hint: Think of every place the copy lives and every time it changes.

choices.text: A write in the index for every write to an item the index holds
choices.why: Yes: the 10,029 orders would cost 10,029 write units more to load.

choices.text: Storage for the projected items, with some overhead per item
choices.why: Yes, at the table's price per GB.

choices.text: Two index writes when an update changes `order_day`
choices.why: Yes: the old entry is removed and the new one inserted.

choices.text: A write in the index for every order line
choices.why: Lines have no `order_day`, so they are never in the index.

choices.text: A charge for each query of the table that does not use the index
choices.why: A read of the table never touches an index.

prompt: Why does the index `pending` hold 722 items and not 34,100?
hint: What does an item need to be copied into an index?

choices.text: Because it is `KEYS_ONLY`, which keeps only the latest items
choices.why: A projection decides which attributes travel, not which items.

choices.text: Because only 722 items carry `pending_since`
choices.why: Right. An index holds the items that have its key, and only those.

choices.text: Because the backfill stopped at 722 on moto
choices.why: The filtered scan of the table found the same 722, so the index is complete.

choices.text: Because a global index holds at most one item per partition key value
choices.why: Index keys need not be unique; all 722 share one `pending_since`.

prompt: After order o-10009 was delivered, the index `pending` held 721 items. What removed it from the index?

choices.text: A delete sent to the index by the program
choices.why: Nothing writes to an index directly; there is no API for it.

choices.text: A nightly job that DynamoDB runs on every sparse index
choices.why: It happened in the same write, not later.

choices.text: The update's `REMOVE`, which took the item out in the same write
choices.why: Right. Once the attribute was gone, the item no longer qualified: the state is the attribute, and the index follows it.

prompt: An index whose key attribute most items do not carry is called a ___ index.
hint: It has entries for few of the items.

prompt: A program reads pages of a filtered scan and stops at the first page with `Count` 0. What is wrong?
hint: What does an empty page mean in a filtered scan?

choices.text: Nothing, because an empty page always means the table has been read
choices.why: An empty page means only that nothing in those items matched.

choices.text: Only a page without `LastEvaluatedKey` is the end
choices.why: Right. An empty page can still carry `LastEvaluatedKey`, and the loop stops only on the missing key.

choices.text: `Count` is always 0 in moto, so the test must use `ScannedCount`
choices.why: moto reported real counts in every capture of this lesson.

prompt: `scan --limit 100` with a filter on 1 October returned `Count` 5 and `ScannedCount` 100. What does `--limit` count?
hint: Which of the two numbers is 100?

choices.text: The items read before the filter
choices.why: Right, which is why a filtered page can come back short.

choices.text: The items returned after the filter, so only five orders exist that day
choices.why: The day has 738 orders; the limit stopped the reading at 100 items.

choices.text: Kilobytes of data, up to the 1 MB page
choices.why: The 1 MB is the server's limit; `--limit` counts items.

choices.text: Read units, so the page stopped when 100 had been spent
choices.why: Units are what a page costs, not what ends it.

prompt: To read the next page, the request sends back the previous answer's `LastEvaluatedKey` as `___`.
hint: The parameter says "start after this key".

prompt: What can a local secondary index give that a global one cannot?
hint: Where does a local index live?

choices.text: Strongly consistent reads, because it lives with the items it sorts and is written with them
choices.why: Right. The second query asked for `--consistent-read` and got it.

choices.text: A partition key of its own
choices.why: That is the global index; a local one keeps the table's partition key.

choices.text: Being added after the table holds data
choices.why: The reverse: a local index exists only if it was in `create-table`.

choices.text: No limit on the size of an item collection
choices.why: A local index is what brings the 10 GB limit with it.

prompt: A table of sensor readings is keyed on `device_id` and `reading_time`, with a local index sorting each device's readings by temperature. Readings are never deleted. What will eventually happen?
hint: Which limit does a local index bring?

choices.text: The index stops being consistent once it passes a size
choices.why: Consistency does not depend on size; the failure is a refused write.

choices.text: Reads of that device slow down, but writes carry on
choices.why: It is the writes that stop.

choices.text: Writes for that device fail at 10 GB
choices.why: Right: once its readings and their index copies reach 10 GB, `ItemCollectionSizeLimitExceededException`. A global index would have had no such limit.

choices.text: DynamoDB moves the old readings to a second partition key
choices.why: DynamoDB never rewrites keys; a collection belongs to one partition key value.

prompt: Quitanda decides, a year in, that it wants a local index on `total_cents`. What does that take?

choices.text: An `update-table` with `--local-secondary-indexes`
choices.why: `update-table` has no such parameter.

choices.text: A new table created with the index, and every item copied into it
choices.why: Right, which is why a global index, addable any day, is the usual answer.

choices.text: A backfill, started from the console
choices.why: Backfills build global indexes added later; a local one cannot be added at all.

prompt: On AWS, put the life of a new global index on a table that already holds items in order.
items: The index is `CREATING` and the table is backfilled into it

prompt: Dispatch needs "orders not yet delivered, oldest first". Quitanda stores `pending_since` only on open orders, with a timestamp. Which read is cheapest?
hint: Which items does each read have to touch?

choices.text: A scan of the table filtered on `attribute_exists(pending_since)`
choices.why: It finds them by reading all 34,100 items.

choices.text: A query on a local index sorted by `pending_since`
choices.why: A local index is per customer; dispatch would need one query per customer, and the table would have to be rebuilt to get it.

choices.text: A scan of a sparse global index, which reads only what is still open, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. Every item it reads is an answer; to have them oldest first, a fixed partition key such as `OPEN` with `pending_since` as the sort key makes it a query.

choices.text: A query on `by-day` for every day of the month
choices.why: It reads every order of every day, delivered or not.
